title: Stabilizing the Dynamic Low-Rank Training
claim: The existing low-rank training method fails under heavy compression because its layers collapse in rank and discard nearly all of the weight energy.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; training curves, rank heatmap, singular-value spectra with shaded discarded tail
description: A three-panel row of empirical plots that diagnose why dynamic low-rank training (DLRT) fails. Panel (a) shows accuracy against epoch. Blue baseline train and test curves sit well above the red DLRT curves. A callout reads 'DLRT under-fits: low capacity', and a double-headed arrow marks a 25.9% gap. Panel (b) is a layer-by-epoch heatmap of rank, with a red-to-blue colorbar from 14 down to 2. Black triangles mark the first rank drop in each layer, and the deeper layers collapse to the minimum rank early. Panel (c) has two log-log spectra for the last two layers. A black baseline curve and colored DLRT curves for different epochs are drawn, and a pink shaded tail past a dotted red rank cutoff marks the discarded energy, labeled 98.8% and 98.6% lost. The eye goes first to the 25.9% gap in panel (a), then to the pink tails in panel (c).
caption: DLRT collapses under aggressive compression on VGG-19/CIFAR-100 (≈69.6% compression). (a) Accuracy curves: DLRT lags the baseline by 25.9% in test accuracy; training accuracy also plateaus far below baseline, indicating insufficient capacity rather than over-fitting. (b) Per-layer rank evolution; ▼marks the first epoch each layer hits its minimum rank—every layer collapses within the first 100 epochs. (c) Singular-value spectra of the last two weight matrices across epochs {0, 10, . . . , 190}. The red shaded tail beyond i > r is the energy that DLRT permanently discards: 98.8%/98.6% of the total ∥W∥2
abstract: Training neural networks directly in a low-rank parameterization is an appealing route to reducing memory, compute, and storage simultaneously during both training and inference. Dynamic low-rank training (DLRT), which confines weights to a rank-$r$ manifold via the Galerkin projection of the gradient flow, is particularly attractive because it identifies efficient subnetworks on the fly without specialized initialization or post-factorization. However, DLRT fails to find trainable networks under high compression. In this paper, we derive the gradient flow of the best rank-$r$ approximation and point out that the offset of DLRT comes from a curvature-coupling term which is large and thus non-negligible under aggressive compression. Guided by this analysis, we propose a stable dynamic low-rank training method, named SDLRT, which maintains a lightweight compensation buffer that reinjects the top neglected singular directions. Additionally, we introduce a negative feedback on the truncation tolerance to stabilize each layer's rank. Experimentally, SDLRT reliably finds trainable subnetworks where DLRT collapses and as a PEFT adapter on DeBERTa-v3, it achieves the best average score on SuperGLUE at only $2.8\%$ parameter overhead over LoRA.
